Objective: To assess the performance of novel qualitative diagnostic criteria using dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) magnetic 
resonance imaging (MRI) to identify the pathologic complete response (pCR) of primary tumors in esophageal cancer after 
neoadjuvant chemoradiation (nCRT).
Materials and Methods: Patients who underwent nCRT, subsequent MRI, positron emission tomography/computed 
tomography (PET/CT), endoscopy, or esophagectomy for esophageal cancer between October 2021 and October 2023 were 
retrospectively analyzed. The DCE-MRI response of primary tumors was interpreted using five grades by thoracic radiologists 
as follows: G1 (compatible with CR), G2 (probable CR), G3 (probable partial response [PR]), G4 (compatible with PR), and G5 
(stable or progressive disease). The performances of MRI, PET/CT, endoscopy, and their combinations in diagnosing pCR in 
primary tumors were calculated.
Results: A total of 52 patients (male:female, 46:6; age, 61.2 ± 8.0 years) were included. Surgical specimens revealed pCR 
(ypT0) in 34 patients. G1 as the MRI criterion for pCR of primary tumors yielded a positive predictive value (PPV), specificity 
of 100% (18/18), and low sensitivity (23.5% [8/34]). Combining G1 and G2 as the MRI criteria increased the sensitivity to 
73.5% (25/34), with a specificity of 88.9% (16/18), accuracy of 78.8% (41/52), and PPV of 92.6% (25/27). Adding the DCE-
MRI results (G1-2) significantly improved accuracy for both PET/CT (from 65.4% [34/52] to 80.8% [42/52], P = 0.03) and 
endoscopy (from 55.8% [29/52] to 76.9% [40/52], P = 0.005), with increase in sensitivity (from 55.9% [19/34] to 82.4% 
[28/34] for PET/CT-based evaluation [P = 0.008] and from 47.1% [16/34] to 82.4% [28/34] for endoscopy-based evaluation 
[P = 0.001]).
Conclusion: DCE-MRI-based grading shows high diagnostic performance for identifying pCR in primary tumors, particularly in 
terms of PPV and specificity, and enhances response evaluation when combined with PET/CT and endoscopy.
Keywords: Esophageal neoplasms; Magnetic resonance imaging; Neoadjuvant therapy; Pathologic complete response

To develop a more practical and reliable method for 
detecting post-treatment CR in esophageal cancer using 
MRI, our study drew inspiration from the application of post-
nCRT tumor regression grading in rectal cancer [11]. We 
utilized the high temporal resolution of golden-angle radially 
sparse parallel (GRASP) DCE-MRI to evaluate primary tumors, 
which is a critical factor for precise tissue characterization 
in free-breathing perfusion imaging. This led us to propose 
a straightforward qualitative grading system for assessing 
treatment responses using post-treatment DCE-MRI in 
esophageal cancer. The primary objective of this study was 
to evaluate the efficacy of this novel DCE-MRI system in 
detecting the CR of primary tumors after nCRT in esophageal 
cancer, with the aim of complementing or potentially 
serving as a decisive tool alongside established conventional 
modalities, including PET/CT and endoscopy.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
This retrospective study was approved by the Institutional 
Review Board of Asan Medical Center and the requirement for 
written informed consent was waived (IRB No. 2024-0114).
Study Population and Treatment
Among the patients who received nCRT followed by 
esophagectomy for esophageal cancer between October 
2021 and October 2023 at Asan Medical Center in South 
Korea, those who underwent DCE-MRI for post-nCRT 
response evaluation, in addition to PET/CT and upper 
endoscopy assessments, were included in this retrospective 
study. DCE-MRI was performed for patients who underwent 
nCRT, provided there were no contraindications for MRI (e.g., 
claustrophobia), and scheduling availability was permitted. 
The nCRT protocol included daily sessions of intensity-
modulated radiation therapy, accumulating a total dose 
of 50.4 Gy over 25 fractions, along with concurrent 
chemotherapy using cisplatin and either capecitabine 
or 5-fluorouracil. At the physician’s discretion, patients 
were allowed to undergo one or two cycles of induction 
chemotherapy with cisplatin plus either capecitabine 
or 5-fluorouracil before starting concurrent nCRT [12].

INTRODUCTION
In the management of locally advanced esophageal cancer, 
the standard treatment strategy involves neoadjuvant 
chemoradiation (nCRT) or definitive chemoradiation 
[1]. Over one-third of patients achieve a pathological 
complete response (pCR) following nCRT [2,3]. This high 
proportion of pCR supports the use of an active surveillance 
approach, which may improve quality of life compared 
to esophagectomy [4,5]. Therefore, precise evaluation 
of the nCRT response is crucial for tailoring definitive 
treatments and streamlining the active surveillance process 
for eligible patients. The Current National Comprehensive 
Cancer Network guidelines recommend 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose-
PET/CT with or without upper endoscopy with biopsy to 
evaluate treatment response after chemoradiation [1]. 
However, the effectiveness of these modalities is limited, 
particularly when used independently. A meta-analysis 
revealed that the pooled sensitivity for detecting pCR was 
only 62% for PET and 1% for endoscopic ultrasound, with 
specificities of 73% and 99%, respectively [6]. Challenges 
such as radiation-induced esophagitis may compromise the 
accuracy of PET/CT assessments. Moreover, endoscopy faces 
challenges in differentiating between viable tumors and 
treatment-induced changes, such as fibrosis or edema. Post-
nCRT endoscopic biopsy, although specific, lacks sensitivity 
in detecting residual esophageal cancer [7].
MRI is increasingly recognized as a promising noninvasive 
method for assessing esophageal cancer, exhibiting high 
sensitivity for disease presence (with a sensitivity of 
92% for pT0 vs. pT1 or higher) [8] and high sensitivity 
for detecting pCR (80% to 92%), with specificity values 
between 55% and 82% [6,8]. Despite the promising pooled 
sensitivity and specificity of MRI for detecting pCR, it is not 
routinely used in clinical practice for post-nCRT response 
evaluation in esophageal cancer. Various methodologies 
for assessing nCRT response in esophageal cancer using 
MRI have been proposed. Qiu et al. [9] developed criteria 
integrating MRI with endoscopy and CT findings, achieving 
a sensitivity of 82.4% for detecting CR. However, this 
method used 12-month progression-free survival as a 
surrogate for pCR, potentially overestimating results and 
incorporating the apparent diffusion coefficient in the 
criteria, which poses practical challenges for small lesions 
with artifacts. Heethuis et al. [10] employed dynamic 
contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI, focusing on the tumor area 
under the concentration–time curve for their analyses. They

MRI Scan Acquisition
DCE-MRI scans were conducted 5–7 weeks after the 
completion of nCRT. DCE-MRI acquired using 3T MRI scanner 
(Magnetom Vida, Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany). 
Axial DCE images were acquired using the GRASP technique. 
To detect regional and metastatic lymph nodes (LNs) 
metastases, both DWI and post-contrast T1-weighted scans 
using the volumetric interpolated breath-hold examination 
(VIBE) technique covered the scan range from the lower 
neck to the upper abdomen (celiac trunk level). Details of 
the protocol are provided in the Supplement.

DCE-MRI was categorized into five grades according to 
the criteria devised in this study (Table 1, Fig. 1): grade 
1 (G1, compatible with CR), grade 2 (G2, probable CR), 
grade 3 (G3, probable partial response), grade 4 (G4,

disease). The analysis of DCE-MRI images commenced 
with independent evaluations by two thoracic radiologists, 
Readers 1 and 2, who had 7 and 3 years of experience in 
thoracic radiology, respectively. In instances of discordant 
assessments, a third radiologist (reader 3) with 14 years 
of experience in thoracic radiology who was blinded to the 
initial evaluations resolved the discrepancies. In such cases, 
interpretation by the third reader was considered the final 
step in the diagnostic performance analysis of DCE-MRI. 
All readers were blinded to the results of the other two 
modalities (PET/CT and endoscopy) and pathologic results.
In this study, which primarily focused on evaluating the 
response of the primary tumor, pCR was defined as the 
absence of residual cancer cells in the primary tumor site of 
the surgical specimens, irrespective of the pathologic nodal 
status. Evaluation of nodal status is limited by conventional 
imaging modalities [6]. However, to support decision 
making in clinical practice, it is essential to confirm the 
overall response, including the complete response of both 
the primary tumor and metastatic LNs. Therefore, we also 
evaluated the overall response by incorporating both 
primary tumor and nodal status and assessed whether 
adding MRI to conventional diagnostic modalities improves 
diagnostic performance. For PET/CT response grading, 
CR was determined by the absence of metabolic activity 
(standardize uptake value [SUV] <2.5) in all previously 
suspected LNs on pre-nCRT, with no new LNs showing 
increased metabolic uptake (SUV ≥2.5) [13,14]. For MRI, CR 
was defined as all regional LNs with a short-axis size <5 mm 
exhibiting no diffusion restriction on DWI (Supplementary 
Fig. 1) [15]. Responses within the N category were 
evaluated by two radiologists (readers 1 and 2), with any 
disagreements resolved through consensus.
Statistical Analysis
Continuous variables were compared using either 
the independent t-test or the Mann–Whitney U test, 
depending on their distribution, and categorical variables 
were compared using Pearson’s chi-square test or Fisher’s 
exact test, as appropriate. We calculated the sensitivity, 
specificity, accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), and 
negative predictive value (NPV) of each modality (endoscopy, 
PET/CT, and MRI) and their combinations for predicting pCR 
for primary tumors (ypT0), LN (ypN0), and overall tumor 
response incorporating both primary tumors and LN (ypT0N0). 
For the analysis, we used two MRI criteria for pCR in the 
primary tumor: DCE-MRI G1 alone, and G1 and G2. McNemar’s 
test was used to compare sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy 
between diagnostic methods, while the generalized score 
statistic was used to compare PPV and NPV [16]. Inter-reader 
agreement was assessed using Cohen’s kappa coefficient 
with (for five categories) or without quadratic weighting. All 
statistical analyses were conducted using R software, version 
4.1.3 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, https://www.
r-project.org), with statistical significance defined as P < 0.05.
RESULTS
Patient Characteristics
Among 107 patients who underwent nCRT followed by 
surgery, a total of 52 patients were finally included (mean 
age of 61.2 ± 8.0 years, 46 males) in the study. Based 
on pathologic assessments of the primary tumor sites, 34 
patients achieved a pCR (ypT0), while 18 patients showed 
a pathologic PR (pPR): 6 at ypT1, 3 at ypT2, 8 at ypT3, and 
1 at ypT4). There were no significant differences in primary 
tumor location or baseline clinical T category (P > 0.05). 
The median interval from completing nCRT to undergoing 
DCE-MRI was 38 days and from DCE-MRI to surgery was 
26 days. Regarding the assessment of regional LNs, 37 
patients achieved a pCR (ypN0), 15 patients showed a pPR, 
12 at ypN1, 2 at ypN2, and 1 at ypN3; consequently, when 
combining the results of the primary tumor and regional 
LNs, a total of 26 patients achieved pCR in both the T and 
N categories (i.e., overall pCR). The detailed characteristics 
are summarized in Table 2 and Supplementary Table 1.
Interreader Agreement in DCE-MRI Interpretation
The interreader agreement for DCE-MRI diagnostic criteria 
of the primary tumor (five categories) between two readers 
was good (quadratic weighted κ = 0.715 [95% confidence 
interval [CI], 0.623–0.806]). Agreement was moderate for 
G1 alone (vs. the others; binary category) (κ = 0.424 [95% 
CI, 0.113–0.734]) and good for combined G1 or G2 (κ = 
0.692 [95% CI, 0.495–0.888]). The inter-reader agreement 
for LN response with DCE-MRI was fair (κ = 0.355 [95% CI, 
0.066–0.645]; Supplementary Table 2).
Performance for Diagnosing pCR in the Primary Tumor
Based on DCE-MRI criteria, eight cases (15.4%) in G1, 
19 (36.5%) in G2, 20 (38.5%) in G3, and five (9.6%) in 
G4. All G1 cases were confirmed as pCR, whereas in G2, 2 
of 19 cases were ultimately determined to have pPR (ypT1)

The MRI criterion of G1 (compatible with CR) alone 
yielded a PPV and specificity of 100% (8/8 for PPV and 
18/18 for specificity) and a low sensitivity (23.5% [8/34]) 
for diagnosing pCR (ypT0). When both G1 and G2 were 
combined as criteria, sensitivity increased to 73.5% (25/34) 
with a specificity of 88.9% (16/18), accuracy of 78.8% 
(41/52), PPV of 92.6% (25/27), and NPV of 64.0% (16/25). 
MRI G1-2 showed a significant improvement over endoscopy 
alone in terms of sensitivity, accuracy, and NPV (73.5% vs. 
47.1%, P = 0.020 for sensitivity; 78.8% vs. 55.8%, P = 
0.007 for accuracy; 64.0% vs. 41.9%, P = 0.007 for NPV). 
However, MRI G1-2 did not show statistically significant 
differences in specificity and PPV compared with endoscopy, 
and in all measures compared with PET/CT (Table 4).

The highest PPV (100.0% [12/12]) occurred when all 
three modalities (PET/CT, endoscopy, and DCE-MRI) were 
consistent with CR. However, apart from the instances of 
100% PPV, the performance of combined modalities was 
generally lower than those obtained using DCE-MRI (G1-2) 
alone. The diagnostic performance of each modality and 
their combinations are detailed in Table 4.
When examining the factors associated with false-
negative diagnoses based on DCE-MRI, in which pCRs were 
incorrectly identified as PRs, false-negative cases were 
frequently associated with a baseline tumor stage of T3 
than correctly diagnosed CR cases (88.9% [8/9] vs. 36.0% 
[9/25], P = 0.017). No significant differences were found 
in the location of the tumor, the time interval between the 
completion of nCRT and the MRI scan, or between MRI and 
surgery (Supplementary Table 3). 
When DCE-MRI results (G1-2) were integrated with 
conventional diagnostic modalities (either PET or 
endoscopy) and used as the primary surrogate for CR in 
cases of PR from the conventional modalities (i.e., cases 
classified as CR by DCE-MRI [G1-2] were considered CR, 
regardless of PRPET or PRendoscopy), the diagnostic accuracy 
improved for both PET/CT (from 65.4% [34/52] to 80.8% 
[42/52], P = 0.03) and endoscopy (from 55.8% [29/52] 
to 76.9% [40/52], P = 0.005). This improvement was also 
attributed to an increase in the sensitivity of PET/CT-
based evaluation (from 55.9% [19/34] to 82.4% [28/34], 
P = 0.008) and endoscopy-based evaluation (from 47.1% 
[16/34] to 82.4% [28/34], P = 0.001) (Fig. 3).

DISCUSSION
Detecting pCR in patients with esophageal cancer 
after nCRT is a significant challenge. Relying on a single 
diagnostic modality often proves insufficient, especially 
when PET/CT and endoscopy results are discordant. In 
this study, using qualitative DCE-MRI response criteria for 
primary tumor assessment significantly improved sensitivity 
(73.5%), accuracy (78.8%), and PPV (92.6%) compared 
to endoscopy alone (P < 0.05). Defining cCR based on G1 
(compatible with CR) on DCE-MRI yielded a 100% PPV and 
specificity. When combining DCE-MRI with PET/CT and 
endoscopy, the highest sensitivity for pCR detection (58.8%)

was observed when at least two modalities indicated CR, 
whereas the highest PPV (100%) was observed when all 
three modalities agreed. However, beyond these metrics, the 
overall performance of these combinations was generally 
lower than that of DCE-MRI alone (G1-2) alone. Moreover, 
the integration of DCE-MRI markedly improved diagnostic 
accuracy compared to conventional methods, with 
significant improvements in sensitivity for pCR (all P for 
comparisons <0.05), with substantial interreader agreement 
(κ = 0.72). For overall tumor response (ypT0N0), MRI-based 
CR (when DCE-MRI results were G1-2 and negative for viable 
LN) showed superior sensitivity (73.1% vs. 34.6%, P = 0.01) 
and accuracy (75.0% vs. 55.8%, P = 0.06) compared with 
PET/CT and endoscopy, achieving the highest specificity 
(88.5%) and PPV (78.6%) when used in combination.
Radiation esophagitis, which affects approximately half 
of the patients, complicates the evaluation of treatment 
response [17]. In patients with moderate-to-severe 
radiation esophagitis, diffuse inflammation complicates 
PET/CT evaluations, making the determination of 
treatment response reliant on endoscopy, which has lower 
sensitivity for detecting pCR and is sometimes inapplicable 
due to significant stenosis of the esophagus following 
radiation therapy. DCE-MRI stands out in such scenarios, 
distinguishing between radiation induced fibrosis and viable 
tumors through differences in contrast agent kinetics. The 
contrast agent is removed very slowly from the fibrotic 
tissue, contributing to its persistent delayed enhancement. 
This is in contrast to the early intense enhancement 
observed in tumors [18]. This allows for the differentiation 
of fibrosis from tumors in the delayed phase of DCE-MRI [19], 
making it an effective tool for this distinction. The visual 
and morphological information provided by MRI, such as 
eccentric versus concentric wall thickening, further supports 
this differentiation, as demonstrated by the improved 
accuracy and sensitivity of DCE-MRI when combined with 
PET/CT and/or endoscopy. Despite its visual advantages, 
previous attempts to detect CR using DCE-MRI have mostly 
been performed using quantitative methods. This approach 
requires drawing a region of interest and post-processing 
using specialized software to calculate variables. Previous 
studies incorporating quantitative assessment of DCE-MRI 
reported a higher sensitivity of 83%–94.9% [10,20,21]. 
Although quantitative radiological assessment of tumors 
can provide a broad range of information, its use in clinical 
practice can be limited owing to the reproducibility of 
the results. In addition, MRI was necessary to obtain 
these results, pre- and post-nCRT MRIs were necessary. 
Indeed, using both pre- and post-nCRT data could provide 
additional information by allowing comparison of various 
aspects of the primary tumor and LN status (such as size, 
morphologic criteria, and quantitative DCE or DWI values). 
However, obtaining and analyzing DCE-MRI scans at both 
time points is not always feasible and requires considerable 
cost and time. Furthermore, when the tumor regresses, 
determining the precise area for delineating the region 
becomes challenging, and the variability in the tumor 
borders (i.e., segmentation mask) between readers can 
significantly affect the reproducibility of the measurements. 
Consequently, the quantitative method has limitations in 
practical clinical applications. In contrast, our approach, 
which is based on visual criteria and a qualitative method, 
can be applied using only post-nCRT MRI. It does not 
require time-consuming post-processing, such as tumor 
segmentation, and has also demonstrated good interreader 
agreement (κ = 0.715), making it easily applicable in 
clinical practice. 
Despite the superior sensitivity and PPV of DCE-MRI 
compared with PET/CT or endoscopy alone, CR was not 
identified in nine cases (false negatives, 26.5% [9/34]) 
using the DCE-MRI (G1-2) criteria. Patients with a higher 
baseline clinical T category (T3) were more prone to 
misclassification. This misclassification likely arise from 
challenges in distinguishing nonviable and regressed 
tumors, or severe esophagitis at the primary tumor site, 
which may present as eccentric thickening from true residual 
tumors. Indeed, all false-negative cases were graded as G3. 
However, PET/CT and endoscopy identified three of these 
cases as CR, highlighting the importance of integrating 
all three modalities, especially given their combined high 
specificity (88.9% [16/18]), for a more accurate assessment 
of T3 tumors. 
Conversely, two cases were incorrectly identified as CR 
based on DCE-MRI (G1-2) (false positives, 11.1% [2/18]). 
These tumors were initially small at baseline (T1 or T2) 
and were confirmed to be ypT1; the regressed tumors were 
difficult to distinguish from normal mucosal enhancement, 
with or without mild radiation changes. In these instances, 
PET/CT or endoscopy was used to label tumors as PR. However, 
when classified as DCE-MRI G1 or G4, all cases (n = 13) were 
accurately diagnosed as pCR or pPR with a 100% PPV, 
including three cases that were erroneously diagnosed 
by endoscopy or PET/CT. Therefore, the DCE-MRI criteria-
based assessment could be an effective complementary tool

alongside conventional diagnostic methods to enhance the 
precision of CR detection in esophageal cancer post-nCRT. 
In contrast, we evaluated the performance of MRI in 
detecting CR in LN (ypN0). Currently, of LN response 
evaluation is primarily conducted using PET/CT [1], which 
has a pooled sensitivity of 89% [6]. In our study, the 
sensitivity of PET/CT was relatively low (69.4%), likely 
due to false-positive results. Notably, the sensitivity of 
MRI alone was significantly higher (97.2%) when a size 
cut-off of 5 mm and DWI normalization were applied. 
This sensitivity exceeds that reported in a previous study 
assessing LN response using MR T2-weighted imaging with a 
2 mm cutoff [22]. However, inter-reader agreement was only 
fair (κ = 0.355), which is consistent with previous studies on 
response evaluation in rectal cancer but remains a specific 
concern [23]. This variability underscores the inherent 
limitations of post-treatment MRI in consistently measuring 
small regressed LNs following nCRT. Additionally, experience 
in interpreting DWI may be necessary, as several previous 
studies suggest that only experienced readers benefit 
from the addition of DWI sequences [23-25]. Although 
incorporating both primary tumor and LN assessments 
slightly reduced the overall diagnostic performance, 
combining MRI with conventional methods (PET/CT and 
endoscopy) still resulted in the highest specificity and 
PPV. Moreover, CR assessment based on MRI demonstrated 
significantly higher sensitivity and slightly better accuracy 
compared to CR based on PET/CT and endoscopy.
Our study has some limitations. First, its retrospective 
nature, single-center setting, and focus on squamous cell 
carcinoma may limit generalizability. Second, the interval 
between restaging and surgery could affect the accuracy 
of diagnostic modalities, as effects of chemoradiation on 
tumor cells may persist after its completion [26]. This might 
have underestimated the performance of each diagnostic 
modality. However, there was no significant difference in 
the time intervals between MRI and surgery for patients 
with false-negative results and those with correct diagnoses 
based on DCE-MRI (P = 0.289), suggesting that timing of 
these events did not disproportionately affect diagnostic 
outcomes. Third, in the absence of pre-nCRT DCE-MRI, 
evaluation of the MR criteria requiring size or morphological 
comparison was conducted using pre-nCRT chest CT. 
Although we aimed to develop criteria applicable without 
relying on either pre- or post-nCRT DCE-MRI, concurrently 
using both MR scans could provide additional, more 
accurate, and reliable information for response evaluation.
In conclusion, we present a novel DCE-MRI-based grading 
system for assessing the response of primary tumors to 
nCRT in esophageal cancer. Our findings revealed the 
high diagnostic performance of DCE-MRI in identifying 
pCR in primary tumors with notable PPV and specificity. 
Integrating DCE-MRI with conventional diagnostics, 
including PET/CT and endoscopy, substantially improves 
diagnostic performance for detecting pCR in primary tumors 
and could serve as a valuable auxiliary tool in evaluating 
treatment responses in esophageal cancer.
